scenario: A university financial aid office awards scholarships to students who demonstrate either high financial need OR high academic merit (or both). A researcher studies scholarship recipients and finds that high-need students are unlikely to also be high-merit students.

data.description: In the general student population, financial need and academic merit are independent. Scholarships are awarded if high financial need OR high academic merit.

question: Among scholarship recipients, P(high need | high merit) = 40% but P(high need | NOT high merit) = 100%. The researcher concludes high financial need and academic merit are negatively correlated among students. (a) Verify both conditional probabilities. (b) Is this a real population-level relationship? (c) What fraction of students receive a scholarship?

ground_truth.explanation: Berkson's paradox via OR-gate scholarship selection. Recipients without high merit all have high financial need â€” their only qualification. Recipients with high merit show need at the population base rate. Apparent negative correlation is entirely an artifact of the award mechanism.

naive_answer: Financial need and academic merit are negatively correlated: high-need students tend to have lower academic merit.
naive_trap: The scholarship criterion creates a collider. Among recipients without high merit, all are high-need by necessity. This creates a spurious negative correlation in the recipient sample.
python_verification:
p_N=0.40; p_M=0.30; p_s=p_N+p_M-p_N*p_M
g_M=p_N; g_NM=p_N*(1-p_M)/(p_s-p_M)
assert abs(g_M-0.40)<0.001 and abs(g_NM-1.00)<0.001 and abs(p_s-0.58)<0.001
